{{Short description|Genus of flowering plant in the celery family}} {{For|other uses of the name samphire|Samphire}} {{Use dmy dates|date=March 2024}} {{Speciesbox | image = Perce-pierre.jpg | status = LC | status_system = IUCN3.1 | status_ref = {{cite iucn |last1=Chappuis |first1=E. |year=2014 |title=''Crithmum maritimum'' (Europe assessment) |volume=2014 |article-number=e.T203487A2766187 |access-date=27 October 2025}}
(Europe regional assessment) | display_parents = 3 | genus = Crithmum | parent_authority = L. | species = maritimum | authority = [[Carl Linnaeus|L.]] }} [[File:Gardenology.org-IMG 2826 rbgs11jan.jpg|thumb|''Crithmum maritimum'']] [[File:Crithmum maritimum 20080801 105452 Getxo 43p3489N 3p0148W r.jpg|thumb|upright|Rock samphire growing wild on a wall in [[Biscay]], [[Basque Country (autonomous community)|Basque Country]], [[Spain]]]] [[File:Crithmum maritimum MHNT.BOT.2008.1.12.jpg|thumb|''C. maritimum'' – [[MHNT]]]] '''''Crithmum''''' is a monospecific [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]] in the carrot family, [[Apiaceae]]. The sole species, '''''Crithmum maritimum''''', is commonly known as '''rock samphire''',{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}} '''sea fennel''' or '''samphire'''.{{GRIN | accessdate=2014-03-13}} It is found in parts of the [[Old World]] and is edible. ==Description== It is a [[perennial]] plant growing to {{Convert|50|cm}} in both height and width. The [[Plant stem|stems]] are woody at the base, fleshy elsewhere and hairless. The leaves are fleshy lobes. The greenish-yellow flowers are borne in umbels. The fruits (seed pods) are yellow or purple and up to {{Convert|5-6|mm|frac=16}}.{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |pages=74}} ==Distribution and habitat== Crithmum is found on coastlines throughout much of Europe (north to the British Isles), [[Macaronesia]], parts of West Asia and North Africa in the Atlantic, Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}} ==Cultivation== In Britain, rock samphire is cultivated in [[garden]]s,{{cite web |title=Crithmum maritimum |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/24479/crithmum-maritimum/details |access-date=1 August 2022 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society}}{{Cite book |author=Phillips, Roger |title=Wild Food |publisher=Pan |year=1983 |isbn=0-330-28069-4}} where it grows readily in a light, rich [[soil]]. In the United Kingdom the uprooting of wild plants is illegal under the Wildlife and Countryside Act.{{cite web |date=1981 |title=Protection of wild plants |url=https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1981/69/section/13 |access-date=1 August 2022 |work=Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 |publisher=Her Majesty's Stationery Office |location=London}} ==Uses== Rock samphire or sea fennel has fleshy, divided [[Aroma compound|aromatic]] leaves that [[Nicholas Culpeper|Culpeper]] described as having a "pleasant, hot and spicy taste".{{Cite book| author=Culpeper, Nicholas | title=The Complete Herbal | year=1653 | location=London }} The plant can be prepared much like [[marsh samphire]] (''Salicornia europaea''); the stems and leaves should be washed and cooked, while the stems, leaves and young seed pods can be [[pickled]],{{Cite book |author=Mabey, Richard |author-link=Richard Mabey |title=Food For Free |publisher=Fontana |year=1975 |isbn=0-00-613470-X}} perhaps in salted and spiced [[vinegar]]. The fresh leaves may be used in [[salad]]s. Dried and ground sea fennel can also be used as a salt substitute.{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}} Sea fennel pickle in [[olive oil]] or [[vinegar]] is a traditional food of Italy ([[Marche]] region), Croatia ([[Dalmatia]]), Greece, and Montenegro ([[Bay of Kotor]]). It is known as Paccasassi del Conero and used as an antipasto, to accompany fish and meat dishes and to garnish pizza and sandwiches. === Nutrition === Sea fennel has nutritional value,{{cite journal| pmid=23944868 | doi=10.3109/09637486.2013.821695 | volume=64 | title=Nutritional and antioxidant properties of wild edible plants and their use as potential ingredients in the modern diet | year=2013 | journal=Int J Food Sci Nutr | pages=944–52 | author=Romojaro A, Botella MÁ, Obón C, Pretel MT| issue=8 }} and is rich in antioxidants.{{cite journal| pmid=18980846 | doi=10.1016/j.plaphy.2008.09.006 | volume=47 | title=Antioxidant activity and phenol content of Crithmum maritimum L. leaves | year=2009 | journal=Plant Physiol Biochem | pages=37–41 | author=Meot-Duros L, Magné C| issue=1 | bibcode=2009PlPB...47...37M }} ==In culture== In the 17th century, [[William Shakespeare|Shakespeare]] in ''[[King Lear]]'' referred to the dangerous practice of collecting rock samphire from cliffs.{{Cite book |author=Shakespeare, William |title=The Tragedy of King Lear |year=1623 |location=London}} Act IV, scene VI, lines 14b-15. "Half-way down, Hangs one that gathers samphire; dreadful trade!" In the 19th century, samphire was shipped in [[barrel|cask]]s of [[seawater]] from the [[Isle of Wight]] to market in London at the end of May each year.{{Cite book |author=Grigson, Geoffrey |title=The Englishman's Flora |publisher=The Readers' Union, Phoenix House |year=1958 |location=London}} Rock samphire used to be cried in London streets as "Crest Marine". The reclaimed piece of land adjoining [[Dover]], formed from spoil from the [[Channel Tunnel]] and called "[[Samphire Hoe]]", is named after rock samphire: people formerly harvested rock samphire from the neighbouring cliffs. [https://www.samphirehoe.com/ "The name of Samphire Hoe comes from the rock samphire wild plant which was once collected from the cliffs and served as a side dish and was inspired by a passage from Shakespeare's King Lear."] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *[https://web.archive.org/web/20020911154650/http://www.bbc.co.uk/radio4/gqt/samphire.shtml BBC] [[Gardeners' Question Time]] – where there is apparently some confusion between the [[glasswort]] (marsh samphire, found in [[Suffolk]]) and the rock samphire (found in [[Dorset]]). *[https://web.archive.org/web/20060924232844/http://www.biffvernon.freeserve.co.uk/samphire.htm Biff Vernon] discusses the common confusion between marsh samphire and rock samphire, and reproduces a poem on the subject by [[William Logan (poet)|William Logan]]. *[http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/s/samphi10.html Botanical.com] *[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18980846 Antioxidant activity and phenol content of Crithmum maritimum L. leaves] *[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23944868 Nutritional and antioxidant properties of wild edible plants and their use as potential ingredients in the modern diet] {{Commons}} {{Edible Apiaceae}} {{Taxonbar|from1=Q14566672|from2=Q1136311}} [[Category:Apioideae]] [[Category:Monotypic Apioideae genera]] [[Category:Edible Apiaceae]] [[Category:Halophytes]] [[Category:Leaf vegetables]] [[Category:Stem vegetables]] [[Category:Botanical taxa named by Carl Linnaeus]]
